alignment.note: Greek ἤρξατο (single aorist middle of ἄρχω) and Latin cœpit are simple verbs of beginning; the Peshitta renders with a periphrastic construction ܘܫܪܝ ܗܘܐ (lit. 'began was'), where ܗܘܐ functions as an auxiliary marking past continuity — a characteristic Syriac narrative idiom.

Greek δεῖ ('it is necessary') and Latin oportet are impersonal verbs of obligation; the Peshitta employs the verbal adjective ܥܬܝܕ with the pleonastic pronoun ܗܘ ('it is destined/about to be'), shifting the nuance slightly from logical necessity toward predestined futurity.
The titular phrase 'Son of Man' (τὸν υἱὸν τοῦ ἀνθρώπου / Filium hominis / ܒܪܗ ܕܐܢܫܐ) is rendered with identical genitive constructions across all three traditions.
Greek πολλὰ παθεῖν and Latin pati multa correspond to Syriac ܕܢܚܫ ܣܓܝ; all express 'to suffer many things,' with only minor word-order variation in the placement of the quantifier.

Greek ἀποδοκιμασθῆναι ('to be rejected') and Latin reprobari are passive infinitives; the Peshitta fuses the conjunction and verb into ܘܕܢܣܬܠܐ (Ethpaal of s-th-l, 'to be rejected/despised'), so the Syriac single token covers both the connective and the verb.
Greek τῶν πρεσβυτέρων and Latin senioribus correspond to Syriac ܩܫܝܫܐ ('elders'); all three denote the same body of Jewish lay leaders within the Sanhedrin.

The Greek and Latin coordinate the three groups with a simple conjunction (καί / et) governing a single preposition; the Peshitta repeats the preposition ܘܡܢ ('and from') before each group, a Semitic distributive construction making the rejection by each party explicit.

The single Greek noun ἀρχιερέων ('chief priests') is rendered analytically: the Peshitta uses the construct ܪܒܝ ܟܗܢܐ ('chiefs of the priests') and the Vulgate the adjectival summis sacerdotibus ('high priests'), both expanding the compound into two words but preserving the sense.
Greek τῶν γραμματέων, Latin scribis, and Syriac ܣܦܪܐ all denote the scribes/legal scholars; the Syriac root s-p-r ('to write, count') exactly parallels the Greek γραμματεύς derivation.

Greek ἀποκτανθῆναι ('to be killed') and Latin occidi are passive infinitives; the Peshitta ܘܢܬܩܛܠ (Ethpeel imperfect, 'and he will be killed') again fuses conjunction and verb into one finite form, replacing the infinitive chain with sequential imperfects typical of Syriac purpose narration.

The Vulgate inserts editorial punctuation (the colon at index 22) before the connective et, marking a syntactic pause between the passion prediction and the resurrection clause; this corresponds to the Greek καί but the colon has no counterpart in the Greek or Syriac, which both proceed without a mid-verse break.

Greek μετὰ τρεῖς ἡμέρας ('after three days') and Latin post tres dies place the resurrection 'after' the interval; the Peshitta uses the dative-locative ܘܠܬܠܬܐ ܝܘܡܝܢ ('and to/on three days'), a Syriac idiom expressing the temporal point of completion rather than a strict 'after,' which may reflect harmonisation with the 'on the third day' formula (cf. 1 Cor 15:4).

Greek ἀναστῆναι (aorist infinitive of ἀνίστημι) and Latin resurgere are infinitives continuing the indirect statement; the Peshitta ܢܩܘܡ (imperfect of q-w-m, 'he will rise') again converts to a finite verb, consistent with its preference for sequenced verbs over the Greek infinitive chain.
